stem: A candidate with long-standing type 1 diabetes and recurrent severe hypoglycemic episodes asks about pancreas transplantation indications. Which counseling point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Pancreas transplantation may be considered for type 1 diabetes with poor metabolic control such as hypoglycemic unawareness
Pancreas transplantation is indicated only for type 2 diabetes without any renal disease
Hypoglycemic unawareness permanently excludes pancreas transplantation
Pancreas transplant is never offered to patients already using insulin

explanation.rationale_correct: Most pancreas transplant candidates have type 1 diabetes with poor metabolic control, especially hypoglycemic unawareness, after many years of insulin therapy.

rationale_incorrect.B: Type 2 diabetes accounts for a small minority of pancreas transplants; type 1 diabetes with metabolic complications is the typical indication discussed.
rationale_incorrect.C: Hypoglycemic unawareness is a metabolic complication that may support candidacy rather than exclude transplantation.
rationale_incorrect.D: Insulin-treated type 1 diabetes with metabolic complications is the typical population considered for pancreas transplantation.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: type 1 diabetes manifested by poor metabolic control, especially hypoglycemic unawareness

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 15 → Indications → A.1.a. (type 1 diabetes with poor metabolic control including hypoglycemic unawareness); PDF p. 825 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Ninth 010200 item; pancreas-indication angle distinct from liver alcohol abstinence (cctc-1058) and SPK suitability (cctc-2038); anchor verified on Cupples p. 825.

stem: When educating the family of a pediatric intestinal transplant recipient about post-transplant feeding challenges, which teaching point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Oral aversion is common before and after intestine transplantation, especially in pediatric recipients
Oral aversion never occurs after intestinal transplantation
Only adult recipients develop feeding difficulties after intestine transplant
Early TPN use prevents all oral feeding problems permanently

explanation.rationale_correct: Oral aversion is a common problem both pre- and post-intestine transplantation, particularly in pediatric intestinal recipients, related to early intestinal failure, limited oral feeding, and prolonged nothing-by-mouth periods.

rationale_incorrect.B: Oral aversion is specifically described as a common post-transplant feeding challenge.
rationale_incorrect.C: Pediatric intestinal recipients are particularly affected rather than adults alone.
rationale_incorrect.D: TPN and limited oral intake may contribute to oral aversion rather than preventing all feeding problems.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 13, Intestine Transplantation → complications → 5. Oral aversion → a.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Oral aversion … particularly in pediatric intestinal recipients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 13 → 5. Oral aversion → a. (common in pediatric intestinal recipients pre- and post-transplant); PDF p. 744 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Eighth pediatric recipient in bank; intestine oral-aversion angle distinct from community infections (cctc-1057) and SOC suitability (cctc-2048); anchor verified on Cupples p. 744.

stem: A coordinator is updating infection-prevention teaching for heart and heart-lung recipients. Evaluate the following statements about toxoplasmosis:

elements.text: Toxoplasmosis is more common in heart and heart-lung recipients than in other transplant groups.
Toxoplasma-seronegative recipients of seropositive donor organs have higher incidence without prophylaxis.
Toxoplasmosis characteristically occurs only after the first year post-transplant.
Toxoplasmosis can mimic rejection and may require endomyocardial biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

explanation.rationale_correct: Toxoplasmosis is more common in heart and heart-lung recipients because the organism encysts in heart muscle; seronegative recipients of seropositive donors are at high risk without prophylaxis; infection can mimic rejection requiring biopsy. Infection typically occurs during the first two months, not only after one year.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also correct—toxoplasmosis may mimic rejection and require endomyocardial biopsy.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statements I and II are also true; statement III is false regarding timing.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false; toxoplasmosis typically occurs in the first two months post-transplant.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → B. Toxoplasma gondii → 2.–4.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: more common in heart and heart-lung recipients … seronegative recipients … seropositive donors … first 2 months … mimic rejection; endomyocardial biopsy

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → B. Toxoplasma gondii → 2.–4. (heart/heart-lung risk, donor–recipient serostatus, early timing, mimic rejection); PDF p. 224 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Synthesized item. Fifteenth complex_combo in bank; third heart_lung organ tag; distinct from lifestyle combo (cctc-1060); anchor verified on Cupples p. 224.

stem: A candidate with congenital heart disease and fixed pulmonary hypertension from longstanding cyanotic shunting asks about transplant options. Which indication aligns with standard references?

options.text: Simultaneous heart-lung transplantation for Eisenmenger syndrome
Isolated kidney transplantation for Eisenmenger syndrome
Intestine transplantation as the primary treatment for Eisenmenger syndrome
Heart-lung transplantation is never performed for congenital cardiac disease

explanation.rationale_correct: Simultaneous heart/lung transplantation is most commonly performed in adults with congenital cardiac anomalies who developed pulmonary hypertension from longstanding cyanosis or shunting (Eisenmenger syndrome).

rationale_incorrect.B: Eisenmenger syndrome with fixed pulmonary hypertension is addressed through heart-lung rather than isolated kidney transplantation.
rationale_incorrect.C: Intestinal transplantation is not the primary option for Eisenmenger syndrome.
rationale_incorrect.D: Congenital cardiac anomalies with Eisenmenger syndrome are a recognized heart-lung transplant indication.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: congenital cardiac anomalies who have developed pulmonary hypertension … (Eisenmenger syndrome)

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 1 → Heart/lung transplantation → 2. (Eisenmenger syndrome as common heart-lung indication); PDF p. 39 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Third heart_lung organ tag in D1; Eisenmenger indication distinct from heart-lung evaluation (cctc-2013); anchor verified on Cupples p. 39.
